newsitem.title: UK: Central bank warns Clarke to cut borrowing, not taxes.
newsitem.headline: Central bank warns Clarke to cut borrowing, not taxes.

text.p: Britain's central bank governor Eddie George has warned Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to resist the temptation to cut taxes in the November budget and instead scale back government borrowing.

The Treasury confirmed on Tuesday that George had sent Clarke a letter containing budget representations, which stressed the Bank's view that savings from spending cuts should not be squandered on tax cuts but used to cut borrowing.
A Treasury spokesman played down the letter's significance, saying: "It's one of a number of Budget representations we receive."
However, the move threatened to widen the gulf between Clarke and George over interest rates and set the stage for a heated exchange when they hold their pre-budget monetary meeting on October 30.
Clarke is under pressure from the ruling Conservatives to deliver tax cuts in the budget, the last before the general election which has to be held by May 1997 at the latest.
A promise of low taxation contributed to the Conservatives' victory in the 1992 election and promises to be a crucial issue this time round too.
The Conservatives still trail opposition Labour by over 20 points in the opinion polls and Clarke's party colleagues are counting on him to help restore a sense of economic wellbeing.
The Chancellor has engaged in the traditional hosing down of expectations ahead of the budget and at last week's Conservative party conference said he would only cut taxes when it could be afforded.

But he kept hopes for tax cuts alive by reiterating the Conservatives' promise to reduce the standard rate of tax to 20 pence in the pound from its current level of 24 pence.The speech won him a standing ovation.
But the Bank of England has said it is concerned the government's deficit is projected to be 4.0 percent of GDP this year, nearly double the forecast made in 1994.

At the time of the last inflation report, the Bank's hawkish chief economist Mervyn King said such deficits were not consistent with hitting the tough inflation target of 2.5 percent or below. Underlying inflation edged up to 2.9 percent in September.
In July, the Treasury was forced to revise up its forecast for the 1996/97 public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) due to the disappointing tax take so far this year.
It now expects to have to borrow a total of 27 billion pounds ($42.74 billion) by next March compared with a forecast of 22.5 billion made at last November's budget.

The public finances remain the only black spot in an otherwise textbook economic recovery which combines steady growth, buoyant consumer spending and low inflation. Both the Bank and the Treasury expected economic activity to pick up pace later this year and that could widen the gulf between Clarke and George over monetary policy.
Minutes of two monetary meetings revealed George wants to see the 5.75 percent official interest rate back up at 6.0 percent.
But few economists expect Clarke to break with tradition and raise interest rates in the months ahead of the election, and also expect to see tax cut in the budget.

"Mr Clarke will probably cut income tax by three to four billion pounds and justify this by claiming he is cutting a similar amount off public spending in 1997/98," said Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs and one of the Treasury's panel of independent advisers.
This would be a repeat performance of last year's budget and allow for a one penny cut in income tax.

But Clarke may find it hard to make the books balance if he remains Chancellor next year. The government already has very tight public spending plans in place and has taken a hatchet to capital spending and defense.
"This means that if the spending targets are hit, the electorate is likely to be aggressively unhappy about its health and education provision in five years' time," said Davies. ($1=.6317 Pound)
